voice.text: Rain falls on a Blue Ridge mountaintop in Virginia. [pause] Where does that water end up? Tap your guess: it soaks in and stays right there — or it races downhill to a river, and maybe all the way to the Chesapeake Bay.

Follow the raindrop! Rain never just stays put — it races downhill. A <emphasis>watershed</emphasis> is all the land whose water drains to one river, lake, or bay. [pause] Two raindrops can land a step apart on a ridge — and end up in different rivers, because each side of the ridge drains its own way.

Virginia's land drains three big ways. Most of the state — the James, the York, the Potomac — drains east, to the <emphasis>Chesapeake Bay</emphasis>. [pause] The far southwest drains into the Tennessee River — and that water travels all the way to the Gulf of Mexico! And a south-central strip drains to the North Carolina sounds.

Now count Virginia's riches. First: trees! <emphasis>Forests cover most of our state</emphasis> — oak, pine, maple — giving lumber, clean air, and homes for wildlife. And under them, deep rich soil that grows our farms.

Under the ground, more riches: minerals, rocks, and ores. <emphasis>Coal</emphasis> from the southwest mountains burns for energy. <emphasis>Granite</emphasis> — hard stone for building. <emphasis>Limestone</emphasis> — baked into cement. Virginia has been mining these for hundreds of years.

And the living riches! The Chesapeake Bay grows famous <emphasis>blue crabs and oysters</emphasis>. The woods hold white-tailed deer and black bears. And the bright red cardinal — Virginia's own state bird — sings in every yard.

Riches are not endless. Use them wisely! Cut a tree? <emphasis>Plant a tree.</emphasis> [pause] And remember the raindrop: whatever we spill on streets and fields washes into street drains — and street drains lead to streams, and streams lead to the Bay, where the crabs and oysters live. Protecting the Bay starts on our own street.
The raindrop race! A raindrop lands somewhere in Virginia. Which way does it flow? Remember the three big drains.
Sort the riches! Mineral, forest, water, or wildlife — tap which kind of resource each one is.
Protect the Bay! Think like the raindrop: where does it all end up?
All done — you know your Virginia! [pause] Now show what you know.
Not quite. Water never stays put — it always races downhill, drain to stream, stream to river, river to bay.
Not quite. Check the ridge lines: most of Virginia drains to the Bay, the southwest to the Gulf, the south-central strip to the Carolina sounds.
Not quite. Ask where it comes from: under the ground is mineral, trees are forest, rivers are water, living animals are wildlife.
Not quite. Resources are not endless — they keep giving only if we replant, protect, and use them wisely.
What is a watershed?
Rain near Richmond flows into the James River. Where does the James carry it?
Most of Virginia's land is covered by…
Which of these is one of Virginia's mineral resources?
Motor oil is poured into a street drain. What happens to it?
<soft>You know your Virginia!</soft> [pause] Well done.
Good try! Let's follow the raindrop once more.
Lesson done! Go read about the Chesapeake Bay, and find one animal that lives there.
